messages.content: Morning. I'm at Harbour Street Grocer for the walk-in cooler call. Manager says it's been running warm since last night. Start a job for me.

Morning. I can help you get the job started. I can’t create a record in your service system from here, but you can open a new service call and note: walk-in cooler running warm since last night, reported by the manager. Use the store name you gave, and leave the cause and repair details open until you’ve checked the unit. That keeps the report clear without treating the reported symptom as a confirmed fault.

Before opening the cooler, ask whether staff have moved or discarded any product, and keep the door closed as much as practical so your inspection doesn’t add heat. Check the controller reading against an independent thermometer, and note whether the readings agree or differ. Record the box condition, product condition, and any alarm history, since those details can help establish how widespread the problem is and when it may have started. Look for obvious airflow restrictions, a door that isn’t sealing, and signs of a refrigeration fault. Observe whether the unit is running normally, and avoid assuming a particular cause until you’ve checked the operating conditions. If product safety may be affected, have the manager follow the store’s food-safety procedure while you diagnose the equipment. I can help you organize your findings or think through the next checks as you go.
Box temp on the display reads 9.4 degrees. Product's still cold-ish but they've moved the dairy out already.

Add the display reading of 9.4 degrees to the job notes, along with the report that dairy has been moved out. Record that the product felt cold-ish, but don’t treat touch as a reliable food-safety check; product temperature can vary, and feel alone can’t confirm it is safe. Keep the dairy segregated and follow the store’s food-safety procedure. Don’t return it to the cooler until its safety has been confirmed.

Verify the display against a suitable independent thermometer, and note where each reading was taken so you can compare them meaningfully. Check the controller sensor and alarm history for clues about when the temperature began rising. Inspect for a door that isn’t sealing, blocked airflow, stopped evaporator fans, or heavy frost, since any of these can reduce cooling. Check the condenser condition and whether the refrigeration system is operating normally. Keep the door shut as much as practical while you diagnose, since opening it can add heat and make readings harder to interpret. Note readings and any changes as the unit runs, and tell me what you find if you’d like help narrowing down the cause.
Condensing unit's out the back on a slab. Model on the plate is CU-3150-HX.

Add that the condensing unit is outdoors on a slab, and record the model shown on the plate, CU-3150-HX. Before inspecting it, keep clear of moving parts and hot surfaces, and watch your footing around the slab. Check that air can move freely around the coil, and look for debris, damage, bent fins, or signs the unit has been exposed to standing water. Note anything that could restrict airflow or affect the unit’s support, but don’t disturb wiring or piping during a visual check.

Check whether the condenser fan and compressor appear to be operating, and listen for unusual noise or signs of repeated starting and stopping. Don’t remove panels or reach into the unit while it’s energized. If the coil is dirty, clean it using a method suitable for the equipment and site conditions, taking care not to damage the fins or drive dirt farther into the coil. If the unit is not running, is cycling abnormally, or you find electrical damage, isolate it only if safe and follow your lockout procedure before opening anything. Compare your findings with the cooler’s alarm history and verified temperature readings. Keep a clear note of what you observed and what remains uncertain, and update the manager on any product-safety precautions. I can help you work through the symptoms as you check it.
Serial is HX21-0847-K. Plate's a bit faded but that's what I can read.

Record the serial as HX21-0847-K, and note that the plate is faded, so this is your best reading rather than a fully confirmed detail. That distinction matters: someone reviewing the service record can see where the information came from and won’t mistake an uncertain character for a verified one. If practical, capture a clear image of the plate and compare it with your written note while you’re there. Make sure the image is readable, but don’t put yourself in a position where you could contact exposed wiring or a hot surface just to get it.

Keep the serial associated with this unit, and keep the plate reading separate from any information you confirm by another method. If any character remains unclear, mark it as uncertain instead of silently filling in what seems most likely. A small difference can lead to confusion later, especially when someone is checking records or trying to identify the equipment. Avoid relying on a guess for follow-up work; verify the detail against reliable equipment information when that becomes necessary. I can help you phrase the note clearly if you want.
Plate says R-404A but there's a retrofit sticker on the side. It's been converted, it's R-448A now.

Understood. Record the refrigerant as R-448A based on the retrofit sticker, and note that the original plate still identifies R-404A. Treat the sticker as the retrofit indication rather than assuming the plate was updated. Photograph both labels, and note any conversion records or service tags you find. That gives the next person a clear trail and helps avoid the original plate being mistaken for the current refrigerant.

Before connecting gauges or adding refrigerant, confirm the conversion details from the equipment records and verify the refrigerant identity using the installed labels and service history. Use tools and charging procedures suitable for the converted refrigerant, and don’t rely on pressure alone to judge charge. Operating conditions and load affect readings, so consider the full system behavior and the manufacturer’s conversion guidance. Watch for conflicting labels, unclear service history, or signs the conversion was incomplete; don’t guess at refrigerant or charging details. If records are missing or the labels conflict, pause refrigerant work until the conversion is confirmed. Keep the unit’s operating condition and the cooler’s product-safety status documented. I can help you think through what to verify in the records or what readings to collect once the conversion is confirmed.
Controller's flashing E27. Never seen that one on this brand. What would you check first?

E twenty-seven is manufacturer-specific, so don’t assume what it means from the code alone. Before clearing or resetting anything, note what the controller is doing, whether the refrigeration outputs appear to be running, and whether there are other alarm or status indications. That gives you a useful picture of the fault as it stands, and may preserve clues that disappear after a reset.

Check the controller’s make and exact identification on its label, then use the matching service documentation to interpret the code. For a safe initial inspection, look for a loose or damaged sensor lead, connector, or communication cable. Check around the controller and terminals for moisture, corrosion, or signs of a poor connection. Avoid disturbing wiring while the equipment is energized, and follow the site’s safe working procedure.

Compare the displayed temperatures with a reliable independent reading. Think about whether the values are plausible and stable, and whether they fit what you can observe at the case. A reading that jumps around or seems inconsistent can point toward a sensor, connection, or wiring problem, but don’t conclude that from the code alone. If the documentation identifies a sensor fault, verify the wiring and sensor type against the equipment information before replacing anything. Don’t change settings just to make the alarm disappear; that can hide the cause or affect control.

Keep an eye on the case temperature and product condition while you investigate. If the case is warming, follow the store’s food-safety procedure and let the appropriate staff know. Avoid repeated power cycling, since it can interrupt cooling or erase useful alarm history. Once you’ve identified the controller and found the code description in its documentation, use that information to choose the next diagnostic step. If you can read me the controller identification and the description for E twenty-seven, I can help you work through what to check next.
Manager's name is Priya. She says text her, don't ring, she's on the shop floor all morning.

Understood. I’ll use text, not a call, to reach Priya while she’s on the shop floor all morning. That lets her read it when she has a suitable moment, without needing to stop what she’s doing or answer straight away. Keep the message brief and focused on anything that needs her attention; a clear opening makes it easier to scan, and putting the key point first means she can understand it quickly. You could write: “Hi Priya, noted. I’ll keep you updated by text and won’t call while you’re on the shop floor.” I haven’t sent it; that’s just wording you can use. If you need a decision, say plainly what you need from her and whether it can wait. It’s usually easier to respond to one clear message than several separate ones, and she may not see a text immediately while she’s busy. If the matter changes or becomes urgent, make that clear in the message, but still respect her request not to ring. I can help tailor the wording if you tell me what you need to update her about.
She wants the cooler back down by 11 am, they've got a dairy delivery coming.

Understood. Treat recovery as urgent, but don’t promise it will be back down by 11 am until you’ve confirmed the fault and seen the cooler cooling properly. Check the controller’s documented alarm meaning, then compare its temperature reading with an independent reading in the space. Look for a loose or damaged sensor connection, blocked airflow, a fan that isn’t moving air, or signs the refrigeration system isn’t operating as expected. Check that the doors are closing properly and that nothing is obstructing the return or supply air. Keep the doors closed as much as possible while you work, since warm air entering can slow recovery and make the readings harder to judge. If product temperature may be affected, follow the store’s food-safety process and raise that concern promptly. Give her a clear update once you know whether the cooler is pulling down and whether it looks likely to be ready for the dairy delivery; if it isn’t, say so early rather than guessing. I can help you think through the alarm or the next checks as you go.
Evaporator's got three fans. The middle one isn't spinning, the outer two are fine.

That points to a local fan fault or a problem with its supply or control, but make the unit safe to inspect first. Isolate power and verify it’s de-energized before touching the fan, connector, or wiring. Check for ice, debris, or anything else obstructing the blade, and see whether it turns freely by hand. Don’t force it; stiffness or scraping can indicate a seized or damaged motor or bearing. Inspect the connector and wiring for looseness, rubbed insulation, heat damage, or corrosion.

If the blade turns freely and nothing is visibly damaged, compare the middle fan’s supply and control with a working fan, using the wiring diagram and safe test procedures. A missing supply may point upstream, while correct supply with no operation may point to the motor or its connection. Be careful not to assume the fan should be running unless the controls are calling for it, and don’t bypass a safety or leave exposed live parts.

If ice is blocking the fan, look for why it formed before clearing it. A recurring freeze-up can indicate an airflow, defrost, or control problem, and simply freeing the blade may only restore operation briefly. I can help you narrow down the checks if you can tell me what you find.
Spun the middle fan by hand, it's seized. Bearing's gone. Motor label says EFM-9W-230, so that's the one to order.

A seized bearing makes the motor a strong suspect. Before ordering, confirm EFM-9W-230 against the unit’s parts information or wiring documentation, and check that the replacement matches the required voltage, mounting, rotation, airflow, and connector. The label alone may not confirm every fit detail, so compare the lead arrangement and mounting points as well. A mismatch can mean the motor won’t fit, may run in the wrong direction, or could create an electrical problem.

With power isolated and verified safe, inspect the fan blade for damage or rubbing, and check that the shroud is clear. Look for ice or debris that could have overloaded the motor, and make sure the wiring and connector haven’t been heat-damaged or loosened. Don’t force the blade or reuse a damaged connector. After replacement, confirm the fan starts reliably and moves air in the correct direction; listen for rubbing or unusual vibration, then check the other fans and monitor cooler recovery. If it still won’t run properly, recheck the supply and connections before condemning another component. I can help you work through those checks or confirm the fit details.
Coil's iced up on the side with the dead fan. I'll put it into a manual defrost while I look at the condensing unit.

That’s a sensible next step. Make sure the manual defrost is authorized by the controller procedure, and protect the stock while the case is out of refrigeration. Let the coil thaw naturally; don’t chip at it or use a flame or concentrated heat. Check that meltwater drains freely and won’t reach electrical components.

The dead evaporator fan can explain poor airflow and ice on that section, so leave the case out of service until the motor is replaced and the coil is clear. At the condensing unit, keep clear of live terminals and moving parts. Look for blocked airflow, a dirty condenser, or a fan that isn’t running; isolate power before cleaning or touching equipment. If anything looks damaged or the unit is behaving abnormally, stop and follow the service procedure rather than forcing it to run. After the repair, verify airflow through the coil, drainage, and stable operation before returning the case to service.
Defrost termination's set at 13 degrees on the controller. Leaving that alone for now.

Leaving the termination setting unchanged is prudent while you’re diagnosing the failed fan and icing. Check the controller’s displayed coil temperature against a reliable probe, and confirm the sensor is secure, properly positioned, and not buried in ice or loose from the coil. A false sensor reading can make defrost end too early or continue longer than intended.

Let the programmed termination do its job, but keep an eye on meltwater, the drain, and the product temperature. Don’t bypass the termination or extend defrost without following the manufacturer’s procedure. Once the coil is clear, restore cooling only when the fan fault is addressed, then verify the fan runs and airflow is even. If the sensor reading seems implausible or the controller ends defrost before the coil is clear, document what you observe and check the sensor circuit and controller guidance before changing settings.
Gauges are on. Suction's 38 psi.

That reading alone isn’t enough to judge the charge or diagnose a restriction, especially with the coil iced and the evaporator fan stopped. The refrigerant type matters, and pressure needs to be interpreted alongside its corresponding saturation temperature, operating conditions, and the system’s metering device. A single suction reading can shift with airflow, load, and the stage of defrost, so it doesn’t tell you by itself whether refrigerant is low or flow is restricted.

Since you’re already in defrost, don’t use the current suction pressure as a basis for adding or removing refrigerant. Keep the case protected, let the coil thaw fully, and correct the fan fault first. Watch for water from the thaw and make sure it drains rather than refreezing or affecting nearby components. Once airflow is restored and the system has stabilized under normal cooling conditions, compare pressures with line temperatures and follow the manufacturer’s charging procedure. Also check that the gauges and hoses are connected safely, and avoid opening the system unless you have a clear reason to do so. If the readings still look unusual after airflow is back, tell me the refrigerant type and the relevant temperatures, and I can help you work through them.
Head pressure 221. Hang on, misread the needle, it's 212 psi.

A head pressure of 212 psi by itself doesn’t tell you whether the system is properly charged. Its meaning depends on the refrigerant, outdoor or room conditions, condenser airflow, and whether the system is operating in normal cooling. During defrost, or with a blocked or iced evaporator, pressures can be misleading, so treat this as one clue rather than a diagnosis.

Confirm the refrigerant from the unit’s data plate, and check that the condenser coil and fan have clear airflow. Look for dirt, obstruction, or a fan that isn’t moving air properly; poor heat rejection can drive pressure up and make a charge adjustment the wrong fix. Don’t add or recover refrigerant based on this reading alone. After the coil is clear and the fan fault is corrected, let the system stabilize in cooling, then compare pressure with line temperatures and the manufacturer’s charging method. Make sure your readings are taken under steady operating conditions, since changing load or mode can shift them. If pressure rises abnormally, or you see signs of poor condenser airflow, stop and address that before continuing. Keep an eye on case temperature while the system is out of normal operation. I can help you work through the next checks if you tell me what the system is doing now.
Condenser coil's filthy, a lot of cardboard dust. Should I wash it before I take more readings?

Yes, clean it before you take more diagnostic readings. A heavily loaded condenser coil can choke off airflow, trap heat, and drive head pressure up, so readings taken in that condition may point you in the wrong direction. Cleaning gives you a more representative operating condition and makes it easier to judge what the system is actually doing. Keep the case temperature in view while you work, especially if the system has to be off or airflow is interrupted.

Make the equipment safe according to the store’s procedures, and keep water and loosened debris away from electrical components and nearby product. Start by removing the loose cardboard dust with a suitable soft brush or vacuum. Work in a way that carries the debris out of the coil rather than packing it farther into the fins. Avoid scraping across the fin edges or pushing hard, since bent fins can reduce airflow even after the dust is gone.

If washing is appropriate for this coil and location, use gentle water pressure and take care not to soak motors, controls, wiring, or nearby merchandise. Avoid harsh chemicals unless the manufacturer allows them; residue or an unsuitable cleaner can damage the coil or leave contamination behind. Watch where the rinse water and dust are going, and make sure the coil can drain without creating a hazard.

Let the coil drain and dry, then restore power and confirm the condenser fan runs freely and moves air in the correct direction. Listen and look for anything unusual, and check that airflow is not blocked around the condenser. Once the system has settled into normal cooling, take your readings and compare pressures with temperatures using the specified charging procedure. If the readings still look off after airflow is restored, you can then troubleshoot without the dirty coil skewing the picture. I can help you think through the readings when you have them.
Condenser fan motor on the condensing unit is noisy and running slow. Old motor says OFM-5512, but the supplier app says it's superseded by OFM-5521. So OFM-5521 is what I'd order.

That sounds plausible, but verify the supersession against the condensing unit’s wiring diagram or parts data before ordering. Make sure the replacement matches the required voltage, horsepower, speed, rotation, shaft dimensions, mounting, enclosure rating, and capacitor arrangement. A supplier cross-reference can be correct for the motor family but still miss an application-specific detail.

Until it’s replaced, treat the slow, noisy fan as a likely cause of poor condenser airflow and elevated head pressure. Shut off and isolate power before inspecting or handling the motor or fan. Check for a dragging blade, debris, damaged bearings, or a failing capacitor; don’t keep running it if the fan is binding or overheating. After fitting the confirmed replacement, verify the blade turns freely, airflow is correct, and the motor runs steadily. Then clean the coil and retake readings under normal cooling conditions.
Compressor's pulling 11.6 amps. RLA on the plate is 14.2, so it's not overloaded.

That comparison alone doesn’t confirm the compressor is healthy or operating normally. RLA is a rating reference, not a target current or a direct overload test. Current depends on supply voltage, suction and discharge conditions, refrigerant mass flow, and the compressor’s operating state.

Since the condenser fan is slow and noisy, avoid judging compressor performance until airflow is restored and the system has stabilized. Check voltage at the compressor while it’s running, compare the measured current with the manufacturer’s data for the actual conditions, and review suction and discharge pressures alongside line temperatures. Confirm the compressor is not short cycling, and check for abnormal sound, vibration, or excessive shell temperature. If the overload is opening, investigate the cause rather than assuming the lower reading rules out trouble. Keep the case temperature and product condition in mind while you work.
Run cap on the compressor reads low. It's a 45 microfarad. I've only got a 40 in the van, so that's no good.

Right, don’t substitute the 40 microfarad capacitor for the 45 microfarad one unless the compressor manufacturer explicitly permits that value. The capacitance is outside the intended value, and a mismatched run capacitor can cause poor starting or running, excess heat, and compressor damage. Use the specified capacitance and at least the required voltage rating, with the correct capacitor type and connection.

Isolate power and verify it’s off before handling the capacitor. Discharge it using an appropriate method and confirm it’s discharged; don’t short the terminals with a tool. Check the capacitor’s condition and wiring, and make sure the replacement terminals are connected exactly as the wiring diagram shows. Once the correct capacitor is installed, let the system stabilize and reassess compressor current, voltage, pressures, and temperatures under the current operating conditions. The fan fault also needs to be corrected before drawing conclusions about system performance.
Contactor points are pitted too. The contactor is a CN-2P-30.

Pitted points can add resistance, cause voltage drop, and contribute to heating or unreliable operation. With power isolated and verified off, inspect for heat damage, loose terminals, or signs the contactor has been chattering. If the contacts are badly eroded or welded, replace the contactor rather than filing the points; contact damage can return quickly, and filing may affect the contact surface.

Use the existing contactor’s markings and wiring diagram to confirm the coil voltage, pole arrangement, and rating before fitting a replacement. Don’t rely on the model designation alone. Check that the replacement is suitable for the compressor load, and tighten connections to the specified torque. After replacement, verify the coil is receiving its proper control voltage and that the compressor sees stable voltage under load. The low run-capacitance reading and the condenser fan fault still need attention, so assess operation only after those issues are corrected.
Compressor sticker says installed March 2021. The unit itself was made in 2019.

That suggests the compressor may have been replaced after the unit was built, but the sticker alone doesn’t confirm why or whether the replacement was covered by any warranty. Record the compressor identification and installation note, and check the service history or paperwork for the replacement details. Also verify the compressor’s electrical data and capacitor specification from its own label or approved service information, rather than assuming the original unit data still applies.

Given the low run-capacitor reading and pitted contactor, address those electrical issues before judging compressor condition. Inspect wiring and terminals for heat damage, confirm the correct replacement parts, then check voltage and running current once the system is operating safely. If the compressor still draws abnormal current, trips protection, or struggles to run, investigate the supply, refrigerant circuit, and compressor condition rather than repeatedly restarting it.
Coil's defrosted. Ice is all gone. Running on the two good fans now.

Good. With the coil clear and the two working fans running, let the system settle and confirm air is moving evenly across the coil, rather than bypassing it or leaving stagnant areas. Make sure the failed fan circuit is safely isolated, and check that the remaining fans are not obstructed, struggling, or carrying more load than they can handle. Listen and feel for unusual vibration or noise, and verify the coil and drain area stay clear as the unit runs.

Watch for an even frost pattern and check that the suction line and return air behave normally. If ice starts building again, consider poor airflow, a defrost control or heater problem, a blocked drain, or an evaporator feed issue. Don’t leave the unit relying on reduced fan capacity if it can’t hold temperature safely; protect the affected product and arrange repair of the failed fan. Also finish checking the low capacitor and damaged contactor before treating the system as ready for normal service. If you tell me what you find on those checks, I can help think through the next step.
Superheat at the evaporator outlet is 4.5 K. That's low, it's flooding back a bit.

Yes, that is low enough to warrant checking for liquid returning toward the compressor, especially if the reading is steady under a settled load. Don’t adjust the charge from that value alone. Confirm the temperature clamp is secure and insulated, and that pressure and temperature are taken at the same evaporator outlet location. Verify the pressure reading is appropriate for the refrigerant and operating conditions.

Check the evaporator feed and control, sensing bulb contact and insulation, and whether the expansion valve is responding correctly. Also consider the current reduced airflow from the failed fan, since coil airflow and load can shift the readings. Keep an eye on compressor sound, suction-line condition, and current. If you see clear signs of liquid return, protect the compressor and avoid leaving it running unattended until the cause is corrected. After restoring full airflow and stable operation, recheck superheat before making any refrigerant adjustment.
Turned the TXV in one and a half turns clockwise. Going to let it settle.

That’s a substantial adjustment, so let it settle before making any further change. The one and a half turns clockwise may take time to show up in stable readings, and changing it again too soon can make it hard to tell how the valve is responding. Keep the compressor under observation for signs of liquid return, such as an unusually cool or sweating suction line near the compressor, and watch suction pressure and outlet temperature together rather than relying on either reading alone.

Confirm the evaporator outlet sensor or bulb is firmly attached, insulated, and positioned correctly. Poor contact or exposure to air can make the valve response misleading and lead you to chase a fault that is really a sensing issue. Because airflow is still reduced, the readings may not represent normal operation; low airflow can change coil temperature and pressure and affect superheat. Avoid compensating for the failed fan by repeatedly adjusting the valve.

Once airflow is restored and conditions are stable, recheck superheat using the same measurement points and allow readings to settle. If superheat rises too far, or the coil appears starved, return the valve toward its prior setting in small increments, allowing it to stabilize between changes. Tell me what the readings and line temperatures do as it settles, and I can help you interpret them.
Found a leak. It's the Schrader core on the suction service valve, bubbles straight away.

That’s a confirmed leak at the Schrader core. Avoid further valve adjustments while refrigerant is escaping, since the system pressure, readings, and TXV response won’t be reliable. Keep ignition sources away, ventilate the area, and follow the refrigerant and site safety procedures. If it’s safe to do so, isolate the system using the approved service procedure and recover refrigerant as required before removing or replacing the core. Don’t loosen a leaking core under pressure unless you’re using the proper core-removal tool and procedure; refrigerant can discharge suddenly and cause injury.

Use a compatible new core and a cap with a sound seal, and make sure the sealing surfaces are clean and undamaged. Then leak-check the valve again after repair, including around the cap. Don’t rely on the cap alone to contain the leak. Once the valve is leak-tight, restore the system correctly, allow operation to stabilize, and reassess charge and superheat with the airflow fault addressed. If bubbles persist, check the valve body and surrounding connections before moving on. I can help you think through the repair and checks as you go.
Subcooling is 8 K. The sticker on the unit says target 5 K.

That reading is above the unit’s stated target, but don’t adjust the charge based on it while the system is leaking or airflow is restricted. Refrigerant loss and abnormal heat transfer can make subcooling misleading, and removing refrigerant now could leave the system undercharged once the leak is repaired. Restricted airflow can also change operating conditions, so the reading may not reflect how the system will perform once airflow is corrected.

After the leak is fixed and airflow is normal, let the system stabilize and verify subcooling using the manufacturer’s specified conditions and measurement points. Check that the liquid-line temperature sensor is making good contact, is insulated from surrounding air, and is located where the procedure calls for it. Make sure the pressure reading is appropriate for the refrigerant, and avoid relying on a single reading if conditions are still changing. If subcooling remains above target under stable conditions, follow the unit’s charging procedure rather than venting refrigerant. I can help you work through the checks if you share what conditions you’re seeing.
Okay so I'll recover, change the core, and pressure test. Walk me through the order of things.

First, identify the refrigerant and follow its safety data and the unit’s service procedure. Shut the system down, isolate electrical power where required, and connect recovery equipment rated for that refrigerant. Recover into the correct cylinder; never vent it. Verify the circuit is no longer pressurized before removing the leaking core.

Replace the core with the specified compatible type, using a core tool if needed, and inspect the valve seat and cap seal. Close the valve as required, then connect regulated dry nitrogen with a suitable regulator and relief protection. Raise pressure only to the manufacturer’s test limit, not beyond the rating of any component. Check the repaired valve and accessible joints with leak solution or an approved detector. Never use oxygen or compressed air.

If the pressure test passes, release nitrogen safely, evacuate with a vacuum pump and verify the evacuation holds using your normal procedure. Then weigh in the specified refrigerant charge, restore power, and check for leaks and stable operation. Recheck airflow and operating conditions before judging subcooling. If you can’t confirm the test limit or isolation arrangement, stop and consult the service documentation.
Isolating it now. I thought breaker 12 but 12 is the lights. The walk-in is on breaker 14 on panel B.

Good catch. Before touching the circuit, verify the panel labeling against the walk-in disconnect or equipment documentation, and confirm breaker 14 on panel B actually removes power to the equipment. Don’t rely on the directory alone; labels can be wrong, outdated, or incomplete, and breaker 12 is the lights, so avoid assuming nearby circuits serve the same equipment. If the walk-in has separate feeds for the condensing unit, evaporator fans, or controls, identify and isolate each applicable source. Some components may remain energized even when the main equipment appears stopped, so check what is actually supplied before opening anything.

Use your approved lockout and tagout procedure, secure the breaker against being switched back on, and verify absence of voltage with a properly rated tester, checking the tester before and after the test. Confirm the tester is suitable for the circuit and use it at the points you will be working on; don’t treat a stopped fan or dark display as proof of isolation. Let affected store staff know the cooler is out of service, and keep the work area clear while you verify the condition. If you can’t positively identify every feed or confirm safe isolation, stop and get qualified electrical help before opening the equipment. I can help think through likely feeds or safe checks as you go.
Recovered. Core's changed. Pressure testing with nitrogen at 150 psi.

At 150 psi, first confirm that pressure is within the manufacturer’s test limit and below the rating of every component in the section you’re testing. Don’t assume that pressure is adequate just because it’s safe; the required test pressure depends on the equipment and the repair procedure.

Use dry nitrogen through a regulator and suitable relief protection. Keep the nitrogen cylinder secured, and isolate recovery equipment and anything not rated for test pressure. Raise pressure gradually, then check the replaced core, valve seat, cap seal, and accessible joints with leak solution or an approved detector. Never use oxygen or compressed air, and don’t search for leaks with your hand.

If the pressure changes, account for temperature changes before concluding there’s a leak. If you find one, depressurize safely before correcting it, then repeat the test. Once it passes, release nitrogen safely and proceed with evacuation and charging according to the equipment procedure.
Vacuum's down to 520 microns. Wait, it's still dropping. Settled at 450 microns and holding.

That’s a good-looking hold, provided the micron gauge is connected to the system away from the pump and you’ve isolated the system from the pump for the decay check. Make sure the valves and hoses are tight, and confirm the gauge is reading the system rather than the pump side. A gauge left on the pump side can make the result look better than the system actually is, so its location matters.

If it remains stable through the standing test required for this equipment, you can proceed with charging by the manufacturer’s procedure. Keep the system sealed while you do that, and avoid opening it to atmosphere; even a brief exposure can bring in air and moisture and undo the evacuation. If the reading starts rising, watch how it behaves rather than rushing to charge. A continued rise can point to a leak, while moisture or a problem in the evacuation setup can also affect the result. Check the connections and isolation valves, and make sure the gauge is responding to the system. If you tell me what the reading does next, I can help you think through the next check.
Charged it back up. Added 1.2 kg of 448A.

Since 448A is a blend, it should be transferred as liquid to avoid changing its composition. Use the equipment’s specified charging method and verify the total charge against the nameplate or service data, allowing for any field piping adjustment. The amount added by itself doesn’t confirm the final charge is correct.

Before judging operation, confirm the evaporator and condenser airflow, clean coils, and check that fans and controls are operating normally. Then let conditions stabilize and assess the system using the manufacturer’s specified method, including superheat or subcooling where appropriate. Compare pressures and line temperatures with the expected operating conditions, and check for signs of a leak around the repaired area. Don’t add more refrigerant solely to chase a pressure reading. If readings don’t make sense, verify the instruments and operating conditions before changing the charge.

What should I put in the notes about the seized fan?

Write only what you directly observed and what you actually did. You could note, “Fan found seized and unable to turn freely. Unit condition and effect on operation documented. The aim is to leave a clear record of the condition, not to guess at why it happened or imply that work was completed when it was not.

Be precise about what you mean by seized. If you verified that the motor itself is seized, say so. If you only found that the fan blade would not turn freely, describe that observation instead; don’t state that the motor failed unless you confirmed it. If you checked for an obstruction, record what you found, or say that no obstruction was apparent. That distinction matters because the person reviewing the note needs to know what was actually established and what still needs diagnosis.

Include related symptoms only if you observed them. That could be unusual noise, poor airflow, or an operating fault, with a brief description of what you saw or heard. If you did not observe a symptom, leave it out rather than making the note sound more conclusive than the evidence supports. Keep the wording neutral and avoid assigning a cause unless you have enough evidence to support it.

Also record whether the unit was left running or taken out of service, and whether anyone was advised of the condition. If you made a repair or ordered a replacement, document exactly what you did. If you did not take further action, make that clear too. A useful note separates the condition you found, the checks or actions you performed, and anything that remains unresolved.

Before closing the note, make sure it gives the next technician a practical starting point: the fan is seized or unable to turn freely, what you checked, what effect you observed, and what still needs attention. Don’t fill in gaps with assumptions, and don’t claim a result you couldn’t verify. If you tell me what you observed and what you did, I can help shape it into a concise service note.
Walk-in's reading 2.8 degrees now. Bang on.

Check that the system is running steadily in its normal mode. Make sure the drain is clear and condensate is flowing where it should. Check that doors close properly, gaskets seal, and no product or packaging is blocking the evaporator or return air path. Look for loose panels or insulation you may have moved, and make sure nothing is rubbing against a fan or interfering with airflow. Don’t leave it represented as fully recovered if it has not yet reached its normal operating condition. Explain what is still being monitored and what change should prompt them to contact service.

Reinstall service-port caps and access covers, secure wiring and insulation you moved, and make sure valves, switches, and controls are left in their required operating positions. Remove tools, old parts, leak-detection materials, and any refrigerant containers or recovery equipment. Leave the area clean and safe, with no trip hazards or exposed components. Take a moment to check that your work has not obstructed access, airflow, or the drain, and that covers are seated so they will not vibrate loose during operation.

Note any parts or follow-up work needed, and make sure the store contact understands whether the equipment is operating normally or still being monitored. Actually, one more thing. What's the best way to clean up a glazed pulley?

For a belt-driven pulley, first isolate the equipment and make sure it cannot start unexpectedly. Use the site’s normal isolation procedure, and verify that the drive is stopped before you put your hands near it. Release the belt tension before working near the drive, and remove the belt so you can clean the pulley without dragging debris through the grooves. Keep clear of pinch points, and don’t reach into a drive that could move or spring back under tension.

Brush away loose belt dust, then use a suitable non-oily cleaner and a stiff nylon or brass brush to remove residue. Work along the grooves rather than scraping across them, and take care not to gouge the surface or leave bristles or debris behind. Let the pulley dry fully before refitting anything. Avoid grease, belt dressing, and aggressive grinding or sanding; those can leave a slippery film, hide wear, or alter the pulley’s groove shape. Don’t use a tool in a way that could catch or damage the pulley. If residue is stubborn, pause and check that the cleaner is appropriate for the materials involved rather than reaching for a harsher solvent.

Check the pulley for worn, rounded, or damaged grooves, corrosion, and signs that it is running out of alignment. Look for uneven wear across the groove faces, since that can point to a tracking or alignment problem rather than simple surface glazing. A pulley that is worn or damaged should be corrected rather than just cleaned, since a fresh belt may glaze again. Also look for any buildup that could keep the belt from seating properly. Don’t assume the surface is sound just because it looks clean.

Check the belt as well. If it is shiny, hardened, cracked, or contaminated, cleaning it is unlikely to restore reliable grip, so replace it and correct whatever caused the glazing. Consider whether the belt has been slipping, running too tight or too loose, or being exposed to contamination. Those conditions can generate heat and polish the belt and pulley surfaces, so cleaning alone may only give a short-lived result. Don’t put belt dressing on to mask slipping; find and correct the cause.

Before returning the drive to service, make sure the pulley and belt are clean and dry, the belt is seated correctly, and the drive is aligned and tensioned to the equipment manufacturer’s guidance. Turn the drive by hand only if the equipment’s procedure allows it and it is safely isolated, checking that the belt tracks properly and nothing binds. Keep guards in place before restoring power, then observe the drive from a safe position for unusual noise, vibration, or belt movement.
